title: Standing and reciting
hook: you stand and recite al-Fatiha, then a short surah

segments.voice: Yesterday: takbir, Allahu akbar, hands raised, the prayer opened. Your line was greater than all of it. Did you finish that sentence in your head, even once? Day one hundred two.

The hands come down. In most schools, they fold over the body; in some, they rest at the sides. The eyes drop to the spot where the forehead will touch the ground. And then, for the first time in the prayer, the person speaks at length. Not a speech. Not a list of requests. A short chapter you first met back in the first week of this path, the one that asks for directions. Standing still, in front of no one you can see, saying it as if someone is listening. Today: the standing.
screen: `THE HANDS COME DOWN.` → `EYES ON THE PLACE OF PROSTRATION.` → `THEN THE FIRST WORDS.`

segments.voice: The standing is called qiyam, from a root that means to stand up, to rise, to stand firm. In it, every unit of the prayer begins with al-Fatiha, the Opening. A hadith in Bukhari is blunt about it: there's no prayer for the one who doesn't recite the Opening of the Book. So a Muslim who prays all five prayers says it at least seventeen times a day. It begins, in Pickthall's translation: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." And at its center: "Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help." Now the surprise. A hadith qudsi in Sahih Muslim, where the Prophet ﷺ relays words from God, says the prayer is divided between God and the one praying. When the person says, praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds, God says: My servant has praised Me. When they say, the Beneficent, the Merciful: My servant has extolled Me. And at the middle line: this is between Me and My servant, and My servant will have what he asks. So the standing isn't a recital into empty air. In the tradition's own telling, it's a conversation, answered line by line. After the Fatiha, in the first two units, the person adds some other part of the Qur'an, often a short surah from the end of the book, like al-Ikhlas, four lines long. At dawn, sunset and night, the first two units are recited aloud by the one leading. At midday and afternoon, silently. Either way, you stand, and you speak, and you are heard.
screen: `QIYAM — TO STAND, TO STAND FIRM.` · `NO PRAYER WITHOUT THE OPENING.` · `MY SERVANT HAS PRAISED ME.` · `THEN A SHORT SURAH.` · then, large: `STAND, SPEAK, BE HEARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand still. Feet a little apart, hands folded or at your sides, eyes resting on a spot on the floor in front of you. If you know the Fatiha, recite it slowly, and leave a small pause after each line, as if waiting for the answer. If you don't know it, say just the first line from Pickthall's translation, praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds, and stand in the quiet after it. The bell holds the time.
Qiyam. The standing in prayer, where the Fatiha is recited, then a short surah. Today's word.
Your line: stand and speak. Once today, before you say something that matters, stand up straight first, and say it like someone's listening. Day one hundred two.

howItsDone: In each unit of prayer, Muslims stand and recite al-Fatiha in Arabic, adding another passage of the Qur'an in the first two units; at dawn, sunset and night the leader recites the first two units aloud.

Hanafi scholars hold that reciting the Fatiha is wajib rather than a pillar, and many hold that a follower behind an imam does not recite it aloud (or at all); the script states the general rule. A Keeper may want this nuance.
Hand placement is covered on day 110; here only 'fold over the body; in some, at the sides' (Maliki and Ja'fari commonly at the sides).
